docs.title: Global Building Inventory (globi)
docs.text:
GloBI changes building footprints (GIS files) into EnergyPlus shoebox models and simulates them at scale.

If you are a new user, do these steps:

  1. Install the requirements. To run without Docker, also install EnergyPlus.
  2. Do the sample-buildings tutorial. Then edit the model in sbem-ui and run it again.
  3. Read the workflow overview to see how the parts of GloBI work together.

docs.title: 1. Input Configuration
docs.text:
• Manifest File: YAML configuration defining the experiment, file paths, and preprocessing parameters
  • GIS Data: Building footprints with properties (height, floors, typology)
  • Component Database: Building components and materials specifications
  • Semantic Fields: Mappings between building categories and properties
  • Weather Data: EPW climate files for simulation

docs.title: 2. GIS Preprocessing
docs.text:
Validates and enriches building data:

  • Filters buildings by area, height, and geometry validity
  • Converts polygons to rotated rectangles
  • Identifies neighboring buildings for shading analysis
  • Assigns weather files based on location
  • Injects semantic context (building typology, age, region)

docs.title: 3. Building Spec Generation
docs.text:
Creates structured specifications for each building:

  • Extracts geometry (footprint dimensions, height, neighbors)
  • Assigns building properties (WWR, basement, attic)
  • Links semantic context and weather data
  • Produces GloBIBuildingSpec objects ready for simulation

docs.title: 4. Job Allocation
docs.text:
Distributes work across compute infrastructure:

  • Calculates optimal branching factor based on payload size
  • Submits jobs to Hatchet workflow orchestrator
  • Distributes building specs across Docker worker containers

docs.title: 5. Distributed Simulation
docs.text:
Workers execute energy simulations in parallel:

  • Each worker processes assigned building specs
  • Uses component database to construct EnergyPlus models
  • Runs building energy simulations
  • Extracts monthly energy and peak results
  • Optionally captures hourly timeseries data

docs.title: 6. Results Aggregation & Collection
docs.text:
Consolidates simulation outputs:

  • Aggregates results from all workers
  • Stores in cloud storage (S3) as Parquet files
  • Versions experiments for reproducibility
  • Makes results available for retrieval

docs.title: 7. Output & Visualization
docs.text:
Delivers results to users:

  • Downloads results to local filesystem
  • Generates interactive D3-based dashboards
  • Provides both Parquet and CSV formats
  • Enables analysis of building stock energy performance

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Scalability: Processes thousands of buildings in parallel using distributed computing
  • Automation: Minimal manual intervention from GIS data to simulation results
  • Reproducibility: Version-controlled experiments with semantic versioning
  • Flexibility: Configurable preprocessing, semantic mappings, and output options
  • Regional Analysis: Designed for urban-scale building energy modeling

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text: GloBI produces detailed building energy outputs, for example EnergyAndPeak.pq. You can use these results for many types of analysis: policy and retrofit comparisons, adoption and willingness-to-pay (WTP) models, emissions accounting, and other fleet-scale workflows.

docs.title: Why this is a separate repository
docs.text:
The WTP workflow needs many inputs that GloBI does not make: retrofit cost and incentive tables, energy prices, adoption curves, emissions-factor trajectories, demographic data for propensity models, and Monte Carlo settings. A separate repository, globi-use-cases, holds these tools. This keeps the GloBI install small, and lets the analyses change on their own release cycle.

Other downstream use cases are in the same repository, with the analysis tools, sample inputs in data/inputs/, and the Streamlit apps.

docs.title: What you will find there
docs.text:
The globi-use-cases repository has tools and a Streamlit app for:

  1. Energy and policy impacts: compare baseline and retrofit scenario files (one pair for each year) for energy and peak differences.
  2. Propensity: calculate the acceptance probability of each building (residential logit with census demographics; commercial NPV threshold).
  3. Uptake: apply adoption curves from JSON, so that buildings adopt over time from propensity and curve targets.
  4. Emissions: combine the adopted floor area and fuel mix with emissions-factor trajectories that you can edit.

In the main app, you upload results, set the configuration, select adoption curves, edit emissions, and run the full pipeline with charts and tables. The sample inputs in data/inputs/ let you use the app without new GloBI runs.

For the full feature list, the scenario editor, Docker options, the data layout and the split_scenarios.py tool, see the README of that repository.

docs.title: Download the repository
docs.text:
Clone the repository with Git. Git lets you get updates later with git pull.

git clone https://github.com/daryaguettler/globi-use-cases.git
cd globi-use-cases

You can also download a ZIP file from the Code menu on GitHub. Extract it, then cd into the extracted folder.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+
  • uv (package manager)
  • Docker Desktop, to run the app in Docker with make run

docs.title: Set up the environment
docs.text:
To run the app on your computer (not in Docker), install the Python environment from the repository root:

uv sync

The Makefile sets PYTHONPATH=src, so that the app and use_cases imports work. Use the make targets below, or set PYTHONPATH yourself.

docs.title: Run the analysis app
docs.text:
To run the app in Docker and open it in your browser:

make run

To run the app on your computer without Docker:

make run-local

make run-local is the same as:

PYTHONPATH=src uv run streamlit run src/app/wtp_app.py

Open the URL that Streamlit prints. The default is http://localhost:8502, so the app can run at the same time as the GloBI results dashboard (port 8501).

The workflow in the app:

  1. Upload pairs of baseline and scenario EnergyAndPeak.pq files.
  2. Set the costs and options in the sidebar.
  3. Select the adoption curves and emissions trajectories.
  4. Run the pipeline and look at the results.

To edit adoption curves and emissions trajectories in a separate app, run make editor. To build and run the Docker image directly, run make docker-build, then make docker-run.

docs.title: globi
docs.text:
The GloBI CLI.

Use this to create, manage, and submit GloBI experiments.

Usage:

globi [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Options:

  --help  Show this message and exit.

Subcommands

  • get: Get a GloBI experiment from different sources.
  • simulate: Simulate a GloBI building.
  • submit: Submit a GloBI experiment from different sources.
  • tests: Test commands for CI and development.

docs.title: get
docs.text:
Get a GloBI experiment from different sources.

Usage:

globi get [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Options:

  --help  Show this message and exit.

Subcommands

  • experiment: Get a GloBI experiment from a manifest file.

docs.title: experiment
docs.text:
Get a GloBI experiment from a manifest file.

Usage:

globi get experiment [OPTIONS]

Options:

  --run-name TEXT         The name of the run to get.  [required]
  --version TEXT          The version of the run to get.
  --dataframe-key TEXT    The dataframe to get.
  --output-dir DIRECTORY  The path to the directory to use for the simulation.
  --include-csv           Include the csv file in the output.
  --help                  Show this message and exit.

docs.title: simulate
docs.text:
Simulate a GloBI building.

Usage:

globi simulate [OPTIONS]

Options:

  --config FILE           The path to the minimal building spec file which
                          will be used to configure the building.
  --output-dir DIRECTORY  The path to the directory to use for the simulation.
  --help                  Show this message and exit.

docs.title: submit
docs.text:

globi submit [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

  --help  Show this message and exit.

docs.text:
Submit a GloBI experiment from a manifest file.

Usage:

globi submit manifest [OPTIONS]

Options:

                                  used to configure the experiment.
  --scenario TEXT                 Override the scenario listed in the manifest
                                  file with the provided scenario.
  --skip-model-constructability-check
                                  Skip the model constructability check.

                                  simulating semantic field combinations.
  --epwzip-file PATH              Override the EPWZip file listed in the
                                  manifest file with the provided EPWZip file.
  --max-sims INTEGER              Override the maximum number of simulations
                                  to run.
  --help                          Show this message and exit.

docs.title: Overheating analysis metrics reference
docs.text:
This page describes the overheating metrics that epinterface.analysis.overheating calculates from the hourly EnergyPlus SQL output. GloBI calculates these metrics only when the manifest has an overheating_config (see section D of the tutorial).

All series must have 8760 hourly timesteps per year. The functions use arrays with shape (zones, timesteps) and raise an error for other shapes.

docs.title: Output tables
docs.text:
The postprocessor overheating_results_postprocess returns an OverheatingAnalysisResults object. GloBI saves four of its tables:

GloBI dataframe key Attribute Function Columns BasicOverheating basic_oh calculate_basic_overheating_stats Total Hours [hr] ExceedanceDegreeHours edh calculate_edh EDH [degC-hr] HeatIndexCategories hi calculate_hi_categories … [hr], one per category ConsecutiveExceedances consecutive_e_zone calculate_consecutive_hours_above_threshold Streak [hr], Integral [deg-hr]

The results object also has a fifth table, zone_at_risk (from compute_zone_at_risk). GloBI does not save it.

In GloBI outputs, each table also has the feature index of the building (building_id, feature.semantic.*, ...) in front of the index levels below. GloBI saves ConsecutiveExceedances only if at least one streak occurs.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• \(T_{\mathrm{db},z,t}\): zone dry-bulb air temperature (°C), from Zone Mean Air Temperature.
  • \(\mathrm{RH}_{z,t}\): zone relative humidity (%), from Zone Air Relative Humidity.
  • \(T_{\mathrm{r},z,t}\): mean radiant temperature (°C), from Zone Mean Radiant Temperature. Only EDH uses this input.
  • Thresholds: heat_thresholds and cold_thresholds in the overheating config. The defaults are 26, 30 and 35 °C (heat) and 10 and 5 °C (cold).

The zone weights \(w_z\) are the zone floor areas. The functions normalize the weights so that they sum to 1: \(\tilde{w}_z = w_z / \sum_j w_j\).

docs.title: 1. BasicOverheating (calculate_basic_overheating_stats)
docs.text: What it measures: the number of hours with a dry-bulb temperature above a heat threshold (overheating) or below a cold threshold (underheating). This metric does not correct for humidity or radiant temperature.

docs.title: Per-threshold, per-zone hour counts
docs.text:
For each heat threshold \(T^{\mathrm{heat}}_k\) and each zone \(z\):

\[H^{\mathrm{over}}_{k,z} = \sum_{t=0}^{8759} \mathbf{1}\bigl[T_{\mathrm{db},z,t} > T^{\mathrm{heat}}_k\bigr].\]

For each cold threshold \(T^{\mathrm{cold}}_\ell\) and each zone \(z\):

\[H^{\mathrm{under}}_{\ell,z} = \sum_{t=0}^{8759} \mathbf{1}\bigl[T_{\mathrm{db},z,t} < T^{\mathrm{cold}}_\ell\bigr].\]

These are the zone-level values: one hour count for each threshold and zone.

docs.title: Building-level aggregates (same thresholds)
docs.text:
For each overheat threshold \(T^{\mathrm{heat}}_k\):

Group column Formula or rule Any Zone \(\sum_t \mathbf{1}\bigl[\exists z: T_{\mathrm{db},z,t} > T^{\mathrm{heat}}_k\bigr]\): the hours in which at least one zone is above the threshold. Zone Weighted \(\sum_z \tilde{w}_z\, H^{\mathrm{over}}_{k,z}\): the weighted average of the zone hour counts. It is not the number of hours in which the weighted mean dry-bulb temperature is above \(T\). Worst Zone \(\max_z H^{\mathrm{over}}_{k,z}\): the largest zone hour count for the threshold. Equally Weighted The row mean over all zone columns plus Any Zone, Zone Weighted and Worst Zone. Thus it is not equal to \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_z H^{\mathrm{over}}_{k,z}\), unless the three aggregate columns are equal to that mean.

The same four groups apply to the underheat thresholds, with \(T_{\mathrm{db},z,t} < T^{\mathrm{cold}}_\ell\) and the zone counts \(H^{\mathrm{under}}_{\ell,z}\).

docs.title: Output shape and meaning
docs.text:
• Index levels: Polarity (Overheat | Underheat), Threshold [degC], Aggregation Unit (Building | Zone), Group.
  • Column: Total Hours [hr].
  • Building rows: the four groups above (Any Zone, Zone Weighted, Worst Zone, Equally Weighted).
  • Zone rows: one row for each zone, with the zone name in Group. The value is the hour count \(H^{\mathrm{over}}_{k,z}\) or \(H^{\mathrm{under}}_{\ell,z}\).

Interpretation: this is the simplest view of overheating and underheating. It counts the hours that are outside the dry-bulb limits, and gives several ways to combine the zones into one building value.

docs.title: 2. ExceedanceDegreeHours (calculate_edh)
docs.text:
What it measures: exceedance degree-hours (EDH) of the Standard Effective Temperature (SET), not of the dry-bulb temperature. pythermalcomfort.models.set_tmp calculates SET for each hour from \(T_{\mathrm{db}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\mathrm{RH}\). It also uses the ThermalComfortAssumptions of the config: metabolic rate met (default 1.1), clothing clo (default 0.5) and air speed v (default 0.1 m/s).

\(\mathrm{SET}_{z,t}\) is the SET for zone \(z\) at hour \(t\) (°C).

docs.title: Hot side (overheat)
docs.text:
For each heat threshold \(T^{\mathrm{heat}}_k\) and zone \(z\):

\[\mathrm{EDH}^{\mathrm{hot}}_{k,z} = \sum_{t=0}^{8759} \max\bigl(0,\, \mathrm{SET}_{z,t} - T^{\mathrm{heat}}_k\bigr).\]

Unit: °C·h (degree-hours). Each hour adds the positive part of \(\mathrm{SET} - T\), and the sum covers the full year.

docs.title: Cold side (underheat)
docs.text:
For each cold threshold \(T^{\mathrm{cold}}_\ell\) and zone \(z\):

\[\mathrm{EDH}^{\mathrm{cold}}_{\ell,z} = \sum_{t=0}^{8759} \max\bigl(0,\, T^{\mathrm{cold}}_\ell - \mathrm{SET}_{z,t}\bigr).\]

docs.title: Building-level aggregates
docs.text:
For the Overheat thresholds:

  • Zone Weighted: \(\sum_z \tilde{w}_z\, \mathrm{EDH}^{\mathrm{hot}}_{k,z}\).
  • Worst Zone: \(\max_z \mathrm{EDH}^{\mathrm{hot}}_{k,z}\).

For the Underheat thresholds:

  • Zone Weighted: \(\sum_z \tilde{w}_z\, \mathrm{EDH}^{\mathrm{cold}}_{\ell,z}\).
  • Worst Zone: \(\max_z \mathrm{EDH}^{\mathrm{cold}}_{\ell,z}\).

docs.title: Output shape and meaning
docs.text:
• Index levels: Polarity (Overheat | Underheat), Threshold [degC], Aggregation Unit (Building | Zone), Group.
  • Column: EDH [degC-hr].
  • Zone rows: the EDH of each zone for each threshold.
  • Building rows: only Zone Weighted and Worst Zone.

Interpretation: EDH increases with both the magnitude and the duration of discomfort beyond a threshold. It does not only count hours. It uses the same threshold temperatures as the config, but applies them to SET, not to the dry-bulb temperature.

docs.title: 3. HeatIndexCategories (calculate_hi_categories)
docs.text: What it measures: the apparent temperature from the Rothfusz regression (heat index in °F), sorted into the NOAA categories. The table counts the hours in each category with several aggregation rules.

docs.title: Step A — Heat index in °F
docs.text:
For each zone \(z\) and hour \(t\), the function converts the dry-bulb temperature to Fahrenheit: \(T_{\mathrm{f}} = T_{\mathrm{db}} \cdot \frac{9}{5} + 32\). \(\mathrm{RH}_{z,t}\) is in percent (0–100):

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{HI}_{z,t} &= -42.379 + 2.04901523\, T_{\mathrm{f}} + 10.14333127\, \mathrm{RH} \\ &\quad - 0.22475541\, T_{\mathrm{f}}\, \mathrm{RH} - 6.83783\times 10^{-3}\, T_{\mathrm{f}}^2 - 5.481717\times 10^{-2}\, \mathrm{RH}^2 \\ &\quad + 1.22874\times 10^{-3}\, T_{\mathrm{f}}^2 \mathrm{RH} + 8.5282\times 10^{-4}\, T_{\mathrm{f}}\, \mathrm{RH}^2 - 1.99\times 10^{-6}\, T_{\mathrm{f}}^2 \mathrm{RH}^2 . \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: Step B — Category index (NOAA, by \(\mathrm{HI}\) in °F)
docs.text:
Category Rule (heat index °F) Extreme Danger \(\mathrm{HI} \ge 130\) Danger \(105 \le \mathrm{HI} < 130\) Extreme Caution \(90 \le \mathrm{HI} < 105\) Caution \(80 \le \mathrm{HI} < 90\) Normal \(\mathrm{HI} < 80\)

Each zone-hour gets one category.

docs.title: Step C — Building-level “Zone Weighted” series
docs.text:
The building heat index for each hour is the weighted mean of \(\mathrm{HI}_{z,t}\) over the zones:

\[\overline{\mathrm{HI}}_t = \sum_z \tilde{w}_z\, \mathrm{HI}_{z,t}.\]

The function sorts this series into the same categories. The result is the Zone Weighted row: the hour count for each category.

docs.title: Step D — Other building-level series
docs.text:
• Modal per Timestep: for each hour \(t\), the function takes the modal category over the zones. If two or more modes tie, it takes the mode with the largest category index, which is the most severe (see cat_index_map). Then it counts the hours in each category.
  • Worst per Timestep: for each hour \(t\), the function takes the maximum category index over the zones (the most severe category). Then it counts the hours in each category.

docs.title: Step E — Zone-level block
docs.text: For each zone \(z\), the function counts the hours (of 8760) in each category.

docs.title: Output shape and meaning
docs.text:
• Index levels: Aggregation Unit (Building | Zone), Group.
  • Columns: one for each category: Extreme Danger [hr], Danger [hr], Extreme Caution [hr], Caution [hr], Normal [hr].
  • Building rows: three groups: Modal per Timestep, Worst per Timestep and Zone Weighted. For each of these rows, the categories sum to 8760.
  • Zone rows: one row for each zone, with the zone name in Group.

Interpretation: the heat index is a humidity-adjusted discomfort index, in the NOAA °F form. Zone Weighted gives one combined heat index for each hour. Worst per Timestep and Modal per Timestep show how often the building is in a bad category when you look at all zones in each hour.

docs.title: 4. ConsecutiveExceedances (consecutive_e_zone / calculate_consecutive_hours_above_threshold)
docs.text: What it measures: each maximal run of consecutive hours with \(T_{\mathrm{db},z,t} > T^{\mathrm{heat}}_k\), for each heat threshold. For each cold threshold, each maximal run with \(T_{\mathrm{db},z,t} < T^{\mathrm{cold}}_\ell\). This metric uses only the dry-bulb temperature, as BasicOverheating does (EDH uses SET).

docs.title: Run detection
docs.text:
The hourly excess for overheating at threshold \(T^{\mathrm{heat}}_k\) is:

\[\Delta^{\mathrm{over}}_{k,z,t} = T_{\mathrm{db},z,t} - T^{\mathrm{heat}}_k.\]

An hour is part of an overheat streak if \(\Delta^{\mathrm{over}}_{k,z,t} > 0\) (strictly above the threshold). Consecutive hours with this property make one run. The run stops when \(\Delta^{\mathrm{over}}_{k,z,t} \le 0\) or when the year ends.

For underheating at \(T^{\mathrm{cold}}_\ell\):

\[\Delta^{\mathrm{under}}_{\ell,z,t} = T^{\mathrm{cold}}_\ell - T_{\mathrm{db},z,t}.\]

An hour is part of an underheat streak if \(\Delta^{\mathrm{under}}_{\ell,z,t} > 0\) (strictly below the threshold). The runs are the maximal sets of consecutive hours with this property.

docs.title: Per-run quantities
docs.text:
For each run \(r\) of length \(L_r\) (hours):

  • Streak length \(L_r\): the number of hours in the run (Streak [hr]).
  • Integral of the run: \(\sum_{t \in \mathrm{run}\,r} \Delta_{k,z,t}\), where \(\Delta\) is \(\Delta^{\mathrm{over}}\) or \(\Delta^{\mathrm{under}}\). Unit: °C·h (Integral [deg-hr]). For a constant excess \(\delta\) over the run, the integral is \(L_r \cdot \delta\).

The runs are in time order for each threshold and zone. The function makes one column for each run, then stacks the columns and removes the empty values. Thus the table has one row for each run. To get the longest streak of a zone, aggregate the rows yourself.

docs.title: Output shape and meaning
docs.text:
• Index levels: Polarity (Overheat | Underheat), Threshold [degC], Zone, and Streak Index (the number of the run in the year: 00000, 00001, …).
  • Columns: Streak [hr], Integral [deg-hr].
  • No building-level aggregation: the table has only zone and threshold rows. It does not use the zone weights.

Interpretation: BasicOverheating counts how many hours are outside a limit. This table shows how those hours are grouped: long continuous warm periods or many short ones. The integral also shows how far \(T_{\mathrm{db}}\) is past the threshold during each run.

Downstream use: if a threshold in OverheatingAnalysisConfig has streak_failure or integrated_streak_failure, compute_zone_at_risk uses this table to flag zones. It counts the runs longer than a limit, or sums the integrals of the long runs.
