docs.text: Aspect BasicOverheating ExceedanceDegreeHours HeatIndexCategories ConsecutiveExceedances Primary variable Dry bulb \(T_{\mathrm{db}}\) SET Rothfusz HI (°F) Dry bulb \(T_{\mathrm{db}}\) Threshold use Config heat/cold °C Config heat/cold °C on SET Fixed HI °F bands Config heat/cold °C Unit Hours (counts) °C·h (EDH) Hours per category Hours per run + °C·h per run integral Building rollups Yes Yes Yes No

docs.title: Install EnergyPlus (native runs only)
docs.text:
Use this page only to run simulations without Docker (the make cli-native ... commands). The Docker workers already include EnergyPlus.

GloBI uses EnergyPlus 25.2.0. The worker image (src/globi/worker/Dockerfile) installs the same version. With the same version, your local results match the Docker results.

docs.title: Step 1: Download and install
docs.text:
Download the installer for your operating system from the EnergyPlus v25.2.0 release page.

macOSLinuxWindows
  1. Download the macOS installer for your chip (arm64 for Apple Silicon, x86_64 for Intel).
  2. Run the installer. Keep the default location, /Applications/EnergyPlus-25-2-0.
  3. If macOS blocks the installer, open System Settings → Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway.
  1. Download the Linux-Ubuntu22.04 .tar.gz for your architecture. The file energyplus_versions.json in the repository root lists the exact URLs.
  2. Extract the file to /usr/local/EnergyPlus-25-2-0:
tar -xzf EnergyPlus-25.2.0-*-Linux-Ubuntu22.04-*.tar.gz
sudo mv EnergyPlus-25.2.0-*-Linux-Ubuntu22.04-*/ /usr/local/EnergyPlus-25-2-0
  1. Download the .exe installer (or the .zip) for Windows.
  2. Install to the default location, C:\EnergyPlusV25-2-0.
  3. Run all make commands in Git Bash (see Install make).

docs.title: Step 2: How GloBI finds EnergyPlus
docs.text:
GloBI searches these default locations:

OS Searched folders macOS /Applications/EnergyPlus* Linux /usr/local/EnergyPlus* Windows C:\EnergyPlus*

GloBI reads the version from the folder name. Keep the version in the name, for example EnergyPlus-25-2-0.

If you installed EnergyPlus in a different folder, set ENERGYPLUS_LOCATION to that folder. To keep the setting, add the line to your shell profile (~/.zshrc on macOS, ~/.bashrc on Linux and in Git Bash):

macOS / LinuxWindows (Git Bash) 
export ENERGYPLUS_LOCATION=/path/to/EnergyPlus-25-2-0

export ENERGYPLUS_LOCATION="C:/path/to/EnergyPlusV25-2-0"

Use the C:/... form with forward slashes, not /c/....

If you have several versions installed, GloBI uses the newest version. To use a specific version, export EPINTERFACE_ENERGYPLUS_VERSION in the same way. You can also add the line (without export) to the .env file in the repository root:

export EPINTERFACE_ENERGYPLUS_VERSION=25.2.0

Note

Set ENERGYPLUS_LOCATION in your shell. The .env file works only for EPINTERFACE_ENERGYPLUS_VERSION.

docs.title: Step 3: Check that it works
docs.text:
Check EnergyPlus:

macOSLinuxWindows (Git Bash) 
/Applications/EnergyPlus-25-2-0/energyplus --version

/usr/local/EnergyPlus-25-2-0/energyplus --version

/c/EnergyPlusV25-2-0/energyplus.exe --version

The output is EnergyPlus, Version 25.2.0-.... Then check that GloBI can find and run EnergyPlus. The commands are the same on all operating systems:

cp .env.local.host.hatchet.example .env.local.host.hatchet   # first time only, see note
make cli-native simulate -- --config examples/tutorial/building.yml --output-dir outputs/tutorial

The simulation takes a few seconds and prints a results summary.

Why the Hatchet env file?

Copy the example file before the first native run. make cli-native always loads .env.local.host.hatchet. A single-building run does not connect to Hatchet, so the example file is sufficient. Later, make hatchet-token replaces the file with a real token for batch runs.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Click a problem to see the cause and the fix.

EnergyPlusVersionError ... is not installed

Cause: GloBI did not find the EnergyPlus version folder.

Fix: check the folder name and ENERGYPLUS_LOCATION.

Warnings like Version: in IDF=\"22.2\" not the same as expected=\"25.2\"

Cause: the generated model has the version tag 22.2.

Fix: nothing to do. These warnings are expected, and the model runs correctly on 25.2.

Results differ from the Docker run

Cause: a different EnergyPlus version is used.

Fix: use 25.2.0 (set EPINTERFACE_ENERGYPLUS_VERSION).

docs.title: Setup Guide
docs.text: This guide tells you how to install the tools that you need to work with the globi repository.

docs.title: What to install
docs.text:
You need five tools:

  1. Docker: runs the local stack (Hatchet, localstack and workers) in containers.
  2. Git: gets and manages the code.
  3. uv: installs and manages Python packages.
  4. Python 3.12+: the programming language of GloBI.
  5. make: runs the project commands. Windows needs a separate install (Step 4).

docs.title: Step 1: Install Docker
docs.text:
Docker Desktop runs the local stack in isolated containers. Thus, you do not install large applications on your computer.

macOSWindowsLinux
  1. Download Docker Desktop for Mac.
  2. Open the .dmg file. Drag Docker to your Applications folder.
  3. Start Docker Desktop from Applications.
  4. Verify the installation. Open Terminal and run: 
    docker --version
    The output is similar to Docker version 24.0.x.
docker: command not found

Cause: Docker is not on your PATH.

Fix: add it: 

export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/.docker/bin
To keep this setting, add the line above to your ~/.zshrc or ~/.bash_profile file.

  1. Download Docker Desktop for Windows.
  2. Run the installer. Follow the steps in the installation wizard.
  3. When the installer tells you, restart your computer.
  4. Start Docker Desktop from the Start menu.
  5. Verify the installation. Open PowerShell or Command Prompt and run: 
    docker --version
    The output is similar to Docker version 24.0.x.
  1. Update your package index: 
    sudo apt-get update
  2. Install Docker: 
    sudo apt-get install docker.io
  3. Start Docker, and set it to start when the computer starts: 
    sudo systemctl start docker
sudo systemctl enable docker
  4. Add your user to the docker group. Then you can run Docker without sudo: 
    sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
  5. Log out and log back in. The group change starts to apply after you log in again.
  6. Verify the installation: 
    docker --version
    The output is similar to Docker version 24.0.x.

docs.title: Step 2: Install Git
docs.text: You use Git to clone the globi repository. The repository is public, so you do not need a GitHub account.

docs.title: Check for Existing Installation
docs.text:
Open your terminal and run:

git --version

If you see a version number such as git version 2.x.x, Git is installed. Go to Step 3.

docs.title: Install Git
docs.text:
If Git is not installed, go to the official Git installation page. Follow the instructions for your operating system.

After the installation, verify it:

git --version

docs.title: Step 3: Install uv and Python
docs.text:
GloBI uses Python 3.12+ and uv for package management. Install uv first. Then use uv to install Python.

macOSLinuxWindows
  1. Install uv:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
  1. Verify the installation:
uv --version

The output is similar to uv 0.x.x.

  1. Check your Python version:
python --version

or

python3 --version
  1. Install Python with uv if necessary:

If your Python version is older than 3.12, or Python is not installed, install it with uv:

uv python install 3.12

For more information, see the uv Python installation guide.

  1. Verify the Python installation: 
    python --version
    The output must be Python 3.12.x or higher.
  1. Install uv:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
  1. Verify the installation:
uv --version

The output is similar to uv 0.x.x.

  1. Check your Python version:
python --version

or

python3 --version
  1. Install Python with uv if necessary:

If your Python version is older than 3.12, or Python is not installed, install it with uv:

uv python install 3.12

For more information, see the uv Python installation guide.

  1. Verify the Python installation: 
    python --version
    The output must be Python 3.12.x or higher.
  1. Install uv in PowerShell:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

About ExecutionPolicy ByPass

The -ExecutionPolicy ByPass flag lets this one command run the installation script from the internet. It does not change your system settings.

To read the script before you run it, use: 

powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | more"

You can also download the installer from GitHub.

  1. Verify the installation:
uv --version

The output is similar to uv 0.x.x.

  1. Check your Python version:
python --version
  1. Install Python with uv if necessary:

If your Python version is older than 3.12, or Python is not installed, run:

uv python install 3.12
  1. Verify the Python installation: 
    python --version
    The output must be Python 3.12.x or higher.

docs.title: Step 4: Install make
docs.text:
macOSLinuxWindows

make comes with Apple's Command Line Tools. Check it:

make --version

If you see GNU Make 3.x or 4.x, make is installed. If macOS offers to install the Command Line Tools, accept. You can also run:

xcode-select --install

Check that make is installed:

make --version

The output is similar to GNU Make 4.x. If the command is not found, install make. On Debian or Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get install make

Windows does not include make, and Git Bash does not include it either. Install make one time. Then run all make commands in Git Bash, not in PowerShell or Command Prompt. The make targets use bash scripts and Unix commands.

  1. Install make in PowerShell with one of these commands:

    winget install GnuWin32.Make     # installs to C:\Program Files (x86)\GnuWin32\bin

    If you use Chocolatey or Scoop, use one of these:

    choco install make
scoop install make

  2. Put make on Git Bash's PATH (winget only; Chocolatey and Scoop do this for you). Open Git Bash and run:

    echo 'export PATH="$PATH:/c/Program Files (x86)/GnuWin32/bin"' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

  3. Verify in Git Bash:

    which make
make --version

    The output shows a path and GNU Make 3.x or 4.x. If it does not, see Troubleshooting make on Windows.

VS Code users

Make Git Bash the default terminal. Open the command palette, run Terminal: Select Default Profile, and select Git Bash. After you change PATH, restart VS Code fully. Open terminals keep the old PATH.

docs.title: Step 5: Install the project
docs.text:
Clone the repository and install the Python environment. On Windows, do this in Git Bash:

git clone https://github.com/mitsustainabledesignlab/globi.git
cd globi
make install

make install runs uv sync, installs the pre-commit hooks, and generates the database client that epinterface uses (epi prisma generate).

docs.title: Environment files
docs.text:
The make commands load settings from .env.* files in the repository root:

File Purpose .env Chooses which set of files to use (AWS_ENV, HATCHET_ENV). Created from .env.example automatically. .env.local.aws / .env.local.host.aws Local S3 (localstack). Committed, no changes needed. .env.local.hatchet / .env.local.host.hatchet Hatchet token. Written by make hatchet-token; not committed. .env.scythe.* Bucket name and worker settings. Committed.

Commands that run inside Docker (make cli, the workers) use the local files. The commands that run on your computer (make cli-native, make viz-native) use the local.host files.

docs.title: Input files
docs.text:
Git ignores inputs/, so a new clone has no inputs/ folder. The sample inputs are in examples/tutorial/. Start with the sample-buildings tutorial.

Put your own GIS files and configs in inputs/. Then Git ignores them, and the Docker containers can see them.

docs.title: Optional: EnergyPlus
docs.text: You need EnergyPlus on your computer only to run simulations without Docker. See Install EnergyPlus.

docs.title: Troubleshooting make on Windows
docs.text:
Do these checks in Git Bash. Click a problem to see the cause and the fix.

bash: make: command not found

Cause: make is not on Git Bash's PATH. Run which make: if nothing prints, this is the problem.

Fix:

  1. For winget installs, add the folder as in Step 4 (/c/Program Files (x86)/GnuWin32/bin). Then run source ~/.bashrc.
  2. Check that the file exists: ls "/c/Program Files (x86)/GnuWin32/bin/make.exe".
  3. Close and open the terminal again. In VS Code, quit and restart VS Code fully.
make works in PowerShell but not in Git Bash (or the other way round)

Cause: PowerShell reads the Windows Path setting. Git Bash also reads ~/.bashrc.

Fix: use Git Bash, and correct the PATH there.

'bash' is not recognized, 'cp' is not recognized or process_begin: CreateProcess(NULL, ...) failed

Cause: you ran make in PowerShell or Command Prompt. The targets need a Unix shell.

Fix: open Git Bash and run the command again.

uv: command not found or docker: command not found inside make

Cause: the tool is installed, but it is not on Git Bash's PATH.

Fix: uv installs to ~/.local/bin:

echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc && source ~/.bashrc

For Docker, start Docker Desktop. Then open a new terminal.

Arguments that start with / change (e.g. /tmp/out becomes C:/Program Files/Git/tmp/out)

Cause: Git Bash converts paths that look like Unix paths for Windows programs.

Fix: use paths relative to the repository root (for example, outputs/my-run), or put MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 in front of the command.

make: *** No rule to make target

Cause: you are not in the repository root.

Fix: use cd to go to the folder that contains Makefile.

docs.title: Results dashboard: setup and reference
docs.text: How to run the dashboard and how it computes what it shows. For a walk-through of the pages, see Using the dashboard. The code lives in src/globi/tools/visualization/.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Command What it does make viz-native Runs on your machine. Loads .env.$(AWS_ENV).aws (default local.host, i.e. the local stack) and .env.scythe.storage. make viz Runs in Docker, with src/globi/tools/visualization/config.toml as the Streamlit config. uv run streamlit run src/globi/tools/visualization/main.py Runs directly; you set the environment variables yourself.

The dashboard is served at http://localhost:8501. Both Streamlit configs (.streamlit/config.toml for native runs, the one above for Docker) set toolbarMode = "viewer", which hides Streamlit's developer toolbar from users.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
Page Code What it does Start here views/overview.py Steps, page links and a glossary Explore a run views/raw_data.py Headline numbers, then Charts / Map / Buildings for one run; a generic view for other parquet files Compare scenarios views/compare.py Baseline vs other runs: headline changes, payback, comparison charts, map Overheating views/use_cases.py Portfolio / Map / Priority list / Correlations from the overheating tables

Shared widgets (filters, headline numbers, run labels, downloads, the map legend and captions) are in views/common.py. The sidebar (data source, Refresh, Settings) is in sidebar.py.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The sidebar's Settings box holds two settings that apply to every page:

  • Energy intensity units: kWh/m² or kBTU/ft² for EUI everywhere (headline numbers, charts, map colours, tables).
  • Map coordinate system: the projected CRS of the footprints. Automatic (default) uses infer_rotated_rectangle_crs_hint, which tries a list of common CRSs on a sample of footprints and picks the one that places them cleanly. Users can pick a CRS from that list or type any EPSG code under Other…. Each map's caption says which CRS it used.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Result tables store energy per m² of conditioned floor area (feature.geometry.energy_model_conditioned_area). The dashboard shows:

  • EUI (kWh/m²): per building as stored; across buildings, weighted by area, i.e. total energy / total floor area.
  • Totals (kWh, $, kg CO2): per-m² values × conditioned area, then summed. Pies, stacked bars and the cost and emissions figures all use these area-weighted totals.
  • Peak (kW/m²): the highest monthly peak across meters.

docs.title: Costs, emissions and payback
docs.text:
On Compare scenarios, the first scenario after reordering is the chosen baseline. Then:

  • Annual energy cost and emissions = kWh per fuel × that scenario's price and emission factor for the fuel. Meter names (e.g. NaturalGas) are matched to the table's fuels by resolve_fuel_factor_key. Fuels without a factor count as zero.
  • System cost = the scenario's $/m² × its total floor area. It's a one-off cost and is never added to annual figures.
  • Annual savings = baseline annual energy cost − scenario annual energy cost.
  • Payback = system cost / annual savings. It's left empty when there are no savings or no system cost.

Map costs are per building (kWh × price), matched to buildings by building_id.

docs.title: Overheating
docs.text:
The Overheating page reads up to four tables per run: BasicOverheating (hours above a threshold), ExceedanceDegreeHours (EDH), HeatIndexCategories and ConsecutiveExceedances. The Overheating metrics reference defines each table, its groups (Any Zone, Zone Weighted, Worst Zone, Equally Weighted) and its formulas. The page:

  • offers the thresholds found in the data, and the Zone Weighted and Worst Zone groups (shown as "All rooms" and "Hottest room");
  • builds every per-building table once per run, threshold and room setting (cached). Table reads, the threshold list and the building-level rows of each table are also cached per file;
  • draws only the selected section (Portfolio, Map, Priority list or Correlations), because Streamlit tabs would compute all four on every interaction;
  • applies the sidebar filters by building_id to every per-building table, then recomputes the threshold summaries from the filtered buildings.

Summary statistics (median, P90, share of buildings) are per building and not weighted by floor area, except Floor area overheating and the floor-area histograms.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
The Filter buildings list is built from the run's feature.* index levels that have more than one value.

  • Numeric levels get a range slider in 5% steps.
  • Categorical levels with up to 50 values get a multi-select.
  • The list is ordered floor area, age-like attributes (age, year, vintage, built), other feature.semantic.* fields, then the rest. Shading masks and orientation are left out.
  • Floor area and the first age-like attribute are selected by default.

On Compare scenarios the filters come from the baseline run and are applied to every scenario by attribute.

docs.title: Using the results dashboard
docs.text:
The results dashboard is a web page for exploring GloBI simulation results without writing code. With it you can:

  • see how much energy a building stock uses, and which buildings use the most;
  • compare retrofit scenarios against a baseline, including costs, emissions and payback;
  • find buildings at risk of overheating, and see where and why;
  • download charts, tables and data for reports.

This page walks through each part of the dashboard. If nobody has set it up for you yet, see Setup and reference, or run this in the GloBI folder:

make viz-native

Then open http://localhost:8501 in your browser.

docs.title: 1. Choose where your results are
docs.text:
The dashboard opens on Start here. The left sidebar is always there: the top lists the pages, and below that you choose where the results come from.

Under Where are the results? pick one:

Option Use it when Simulation store Your runs went through the GloBI stack. Every finished run is listed, with nothing to download first. The grey badge shows which store you're connected to. Folder on this computer Someone sent you result files, or you fetched them with get experiment. Type the folder that holds the run folders (usually outputs).

Press Refresh when new runs have finished and you want to see them.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Open Settings in the sidebar to set two things once for every page:

  • Energy intensity units: kWh/m² or kBTU/ft².
  • Map coordinate system: leave it on Automatic, which guesses from the building footprints. Change it only if buildings appear in the wrong place (see Troubleshooting).

What the numbers mean

The What the numbers mean box on the Start page explains every energy term the dashboard uses (energy use intensity, peak demand, payback, …). The Overheating page has its own box for overheating terms.

docs.title: 2. Explore a run
docs.text:
Open Explore a run in the sidebar and pick a run from the Run list. Runs are named scenario (version) · experiment, e.g. Baseline (v1.2.0) · GloBI_Tutorial.

The four numbers at the top summarise the run:

  • Buildings: how many buildings are included.
  • Floor area: their total heated or cooled floor area.
  • Energy use intensity (EUI): energy used per m² of floor area in a year. Large buildings count for more than small ones, so this is the stock-wide average.
  • Annual energy: total energy used in a year.

Below them, choose a view: Charts, Map or Buildings. Only the chosen view is drawn, which keeps the page quick on large runs.

Charts has:

  • how EUI and peak demand are spread across buildings (taller bars mean more buildings at that value);
  • what the energy is used for (heating, cooling, lighting, …) and which fuels supply it;
  • how both vary month by month.

Hover over any chart to see exact values. Download charts and data at the bottom saves every chart (as an interactive web page) and its numbers (as CSV) in one zip.

docs.title: Filter buildings
docs.text:
Use Filter buildings in the sidebar to focus on part of the stock. Floor area and building age are offered first when the run has them. Add any other attribute (typology, heating system, income, …) from the Filter by list.

  • Ranges such as floor area use a slider. Each step is 5% of the buildings, so you can pick "the smallest quarter" even when a few very large buildings exist.
  • Categories such as age bracket use a list. Leave it empty to include everything.

A grey line under the run name tells you how many buildings are left, e.g. Showing 32 of 100 buildings, and the headline numbers update:

Every number, chart, map and table on the page then uses only those buildings. Filters work the same way on the Compare and Overheating pages.

docs.title: Map
docs.text:
The Map view shows each building where it stands, coloured by the measure you choose under Colour by.

  • Hover over a building to see its ID and value.
  • Scroll to zoom. Drag to move. Right-drag, or Ctrl-drag, to tilt and rotate the 3D view.
  • The colour bar under the map shows the range of values. Colours stretch from the 5th to the 95th percentile, so a handful of extreme buildings doesn't wash out the rest.
  • The caption says how many buildings are on the map, and how many very large buildings (over 10,000 m²) were left off so they don't hide the rest.
  • To save the map, press Prepare map download, then Download map (HTML). The file opens in any browser.

If buildings appear in the wrong place, or the map is empty, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Buildings table
docs.text:
The Buildings view lists buildings with the highest EUI first, alongside their attributes.

  • Click a column header to sort by it.
  • Hover over the table and use the magnifying glass in its corner to search, e.g. for a building ID.
  • Download table (CSV) saves every filtered building, even when the page shows only the first 10,000. The file opens in Excel.

docs.title: 3. Compare scenarios
docs.text:
Open Compare scenarios to see what a retrofit (or any other change) does compared with today's buildings.

  1. Pick two or more runs under Scenarios.
  2. Choose the Baseline: the scenario the others are measured against, usually the current stock.
  3. Optionally, give scenarios shorter names for the charts in the first table.
  4. Optionally, switch on Include costs and emissions. Double-click any white cell to change it:
  5. System cost ($/m²) in the first table: the one-off cost of each scenario per m² of floor area, e.g. what the retrofit costs to install. Leave the baseline at 0.
  6. Fuel prices ($/kWh) and Emission factors (kg CO2/kWh): one row per scenario, so a scenario can use different tariffs or a cleaner grid. The starting values are placeholders, so replace them with your local figures.
  7. Press Compare.

Each scenario gets a row of numbers, and the coloured tags show the change against the baseline. Green means lower than the baseline (less energy, cost or emissions); red means higher.

Payback (years) is how many years the yearly energy-cost savings take to repay the system cost. It shows "—" for the baseline, when no system cost is entered, or when a scenario doesn't save money.

Further down the page:

  • Energy use intensity across buildings overlays each scenario's spread of EUI. A curve further left means buildings use less energy per m².
  • End uses and Fuels show each scenario's mix, first as shares and then in kWh per year. For example, a heat-pump retrofit moves the fuel share from natural gas to electricity.
  • With costs switched on, bar charts compare annual energy cost and emissions.
  • Download charts and data saves all of these, plus a cost and emissions summary table.

At the bottom, a Map shows any scenario. With costs on, you can also colour it by annual energy cost, emissions or system cost.

Scenarios with different buildings

If the scenarios don't cover the same number of buildings, the page shows a warning. Totals (annual energy, cost, emissions) aren't comparable then, because one scenario simply has fewer buildings. Compare energy use intensity instead, or check that the runs used the same building set.

About these screenshots

The Compare and Overheating screenshots use the larger TestRegion_Tutorial sample. With the tutorial's own GloBI_Tutorial runs the pages look the same.

docs.title: 4. Overheating
docs.text:
Open Overheating to see which buildings get too warm, for how long, where they are, and what they have in common. This page needs runs with overheating results; see the tutorial for how to produce them.

At the top:

  • Run: only runs with overheating results are listed.
  • Temperature threshold (°C): the temperatures the run was simulated with. Everything below is "above this temperature".
  • Across a building's rooms: buildings have several rooms (zones). All rooms (zone weighted) averages them by floor area; Hottest room (worst zone) uses the worst room, which matters when a single room can be dangerous.
  • What these measures mean explains the overheating terms in plain language: hours above threshold, degree-hours (EDH), heat-index caution hours, longest streak, median and P90. For the formulas, see the Overheating metrics reference.

Then choose a section: Portfolio, Map, Priority list or Correlations. Only the chosen section is drawn, so switching is quick even for large stocks.

A run may not include every overheating table. Charts and numbers for a missing table are simply left out.

docs.title: Portfolio: how bad is it overall?
docs.text:
• Distribution charts at every threshold: one curve per temperature, from yellow (lowest threshold) to red (highest). Curves moving left as the threshold rises is expected; how far they move shows how sensitive the result is to the threshold you pick. The How is … calculated? boxes under each chart give the formula.
  • Headline numbers for the chosen temperature:
  • Buildings overheating and Floor area overheating: the share with at least one hour above the threshold.
  • Typical hours above threshold and Typical degree-hours (EDH): the median building.
  • Hottest-room EDH, top 10%: in each building's worst room; 9 in 10 buildings are below this.
  • Heat-index caution hours: average hours per building at NOAA Caution or worse.
  • Worst-zone vs zone-weighted (scatter): each dot is a building. Dots on the diagonal overheat evenly across rooms; dots well above it have one or two hot rooms, which a targeted fix (shading, ventilation in that room) may solve.
  • Metric distributions: histograms of each measure across buildings, with the median and P90 marked. Switch Y-axis to Floor area to see how much floor area, rather than how many buildings, sits in each band.
  • Threshold sensitivity: the dot is the median building and the bar the middle half of buildings (25th to 75th percentile) at each threshold. A steep line means the answer depends heavily on which threshold you report. Open Per-building threshold fan to see individual buildings.
  • Heat index hours by building: one bar per building (up to 200, worst first), split into NOAA heat-index bands from Normal to Extreme Danger. Labels show the end of each building ID; hover a bar for the full ID. Scroll inside the chart to see more buildings.

docs.title: Map: where are the hot buildings?
docs.text:
• Colour by chooses the measure: degree-hours, hours above the threshold, or heat-index caution hours. The page-level threshold and room setting apply.
  • The 3D building map works like the one on Explore a run: hover for a building's value, scroll to zoom, right-drag to tilt.
  • Overview of spatial distribution: drag the slider to pick a range of values. The histogram highlights that range, and the plan view next to it shows only those buildings, e.g. the worst 10%, to see whether they cluster.
  • When colouring by something other than hours, a second panel below does the same for total hours above the threshold.
  • If every building has the same value (for example, none overheats at a high threshold), the page says so instead of showing a slider. Try a lower temperature.

docs.title: Priority list: which buildings first?
docs.text:
• Top N buildings and Sort by choose how many buildings to list and by which measure.
  • The bars make it easy to compare buildings at a glance.
  • Rankings differ is ticked when a building ranks very differently by degree-hours and by hours above the threshold. High degree-hours with few hours means short, intense heat; the reverse means long, mild overheating. They call for different fixes, so check these buildings before choosing one.
  • Download table (CSV) saves the list.

docs.title: Correlations: what do hot buildings have in common?
docs.text:
• Design and overheating risk relationships: box plots of degree-hours for each building characteristic (e.g. typology, age, wall type). This needs the run's building characteristics file (buildings.parquet); without it the page says so and skips these charts.
  • EUI vs overheating metrics: each dot is a building. The dashed lines mark the averages:
  • top-left: low overheating but high energy use, e.g. comfort bought with cooling;
  • bottom-right: efficient but at risk of overheating, often the group to watch after a retrofit;
  • top-right: both a problem.
  • EDH by number of floors: whether taller or shorter buildings overheat more.
  • Parallel coordinates (expand to view): each line is one building across several measures at once, useful for spotting buildings that are bad on everything.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
Where Button What you get Explore a run → Charts Download charts and data A zip with every chart as an interactive web page (HTML) and its numbers as CSV Explore a run → Map Prepare map download, then Download map (HTML) The 3D map as a web page that opens in any browser Explore a run → Buildings Download table (CSV) Every filtered building with its results and attributes Compare scenarios Download charts and data A zip with the comparison charts, end-use and fuel totals, and the cost/emissions summary Overheating → Priority list Download table (CSV) The ranked buildings with all their overheating measures

Downloads always reflect the current filters.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Click a problem to see the cause and the fix.

No runs are listed

Cause: with Simulation store, the local GloBI stack isn't running (the sidebar shows a red message about reaching the store), or the dashboard was started without the store settings. With Folder on this computer, the folder doesn't contain run folders.

Fix:

  1. Simulation store: start the stack with make engine, then press Refresh. If the message says the store isn't configured, start the dashboard with make viz-native rather than calling Streamlit directly.
  2. Folder on this computer: pick the folder that contains the run folders (usually outputs). Each run folder needs a results file such as EnergyAndPeak.pq.
The map is empty or in the wrong place

Cause: building footprints are stored in a map projection that the result files don't record. The dashboard guesses it from the footprints, and each map's caption says which one it used.

Fix: open Settings in the sidebar and, under Map coordinate system, pick the projection used when the buildings were prepared, e.g. EPSG:32619 for eastern Massachusetts in UTM. Use Other… to type any EPSG code. Whoever ran the simulations can find it as cart_crs in the run configuration.

Overheating says there are no runs with overheating results

Cause: overheating results are only produced when the run's manifest includes an overheating_config. With Folder on this computer, the overheating tables are not downloaded by default.

Fix:

  1. Use Simulation store, which fetches the overheating tables automatically.
  2. Or, with Folder on this computer, fetch them yourself, e.g. make cli-native get experiment -- --run-name <run name> --dataframe-key BasicOverheating. Repeat with ExceedanceDegreeHours, HeatIndexCategories and ConsecutiveExceedances to get every chart.
The page is slow

Cause: very large runs (around 100,000 buildings) take some seconds to load the first time. Maps of many buildings take longest, because every building is sent to your browser.

Fix: filter to the buildings you care about. After the first load, changing a setting is quick.

docs.title: Tutorial: edit the model in sbem-ui
docs.text:
A GloBI model has four inputs:

Input File in the tutorial What it holds GIS file buildings-100.geojson Building footprints and their attributes Semantic fields semantic-fields.yml The attributes that describe a building (Typology, Age_bracket, ...) and their allowed values Component map component-map.yml Which semantic fields choose each part of the energy model Component library components-lib.db The parts themselves: constructions, windows, lighting, setpoints, HVAC, schedules

sbem-ui is a browser app with one page for each input. In this tutorial, you open the sample-buildings model in sbem-ui and make one change on each page. Then you run the buildings again with your edited model.

Experimental

Ask the GloBI team for access to sbem-ui before you start. The sbem-ui repository is private, and the app is under active development.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Complete section A of the sample-buildings tutorial (one building). The batch run in step 8 also needs section B (100 buildings).
  • Install Node.js 18 or newer. To check the version, run node --version.
  • Clone sbem-ui next to your globi folder. The two folders must be in the same parent folder:
your-folder/
├── globi/
└── sbem-ui/

Windows: use Git Bash

Run all commands on this page in Git Bash, as in the main tutorial. If make is not found, see Troubleshooting make on Windows.

docs.title: Step 1: Install sbem-ui
docs.text:
cd sbem-ui
make setup

make setup installs the Python environment (with GloBI from ../globi), generates the database client and installs the frontend packages. The first time, it takes a few minutes.

sbem-ui uses the same epinterface version as GloBI. Thus GloBI can read a model that you edit in sbem-ui.

docs.title: Step 2: Copy the tutorial model
docs.text:
Edit a copy, not the original tutorial files. From the globi folder, run:

cp -r examples/tutorial/sbem-project inputs/my-model
cp tests/data/e2e/components-lib.db tests/data/e2e/semantic-fields.yml tests/data/e2e/component-map.yml inputs/my-model/

The folder inputs/my-model/ now contains these files:

File Used by Purpose project.json sbem-ui Marks the folder as an sbem-ui project and tells it which files to edit semantic-fields.yml, component-map.yml, components-lib.db both The model you edit building.yml, artifacts.yml, manifest.yml globi Configs for running one building or the batch with this model

The folder is in inputs/ because the Docker workers can only see some folders, and inputs/ is one of them.

docs.title: Step 3: Open the model in sbem-ui
docs.text:
1. Start sbem-ui from the sbem-ui folder:
make dev

Keep this terminal open. The app runs at http://localhost:5173, and its backend uses port 8000. To stop the app, press Ctrl+C.

  1. Open http://localhost:5173. On Open a project, select Open existing.
  2. Enter the Folder path of your copy. The path must be absolute. To get it, run pwd in the globi folder and add /inputs/my-model.
macOS / Linux:  /Users/you/your-folder/globi/inputs/my-model
Windows:        C:/Users/you/your-folder/globi/inputs/my-model

On Windows, run pwd -W in Git Bash to get the path in the C:/... form.

  1. Click Open project. The sidebar shows the pages. This tutorial uses the first four pages.

This tutorial does not cover the other pages (Prior Trees, Retrofits, Sampling, Model Execution). These pages are for stochastic models.

docs.title: Step 4: GIS Cleaning
docs.text:
The GIS Cleaning page checks that your GIS file has the columns that GloBI needs.

  1. Under 1. Upload GIS data, select examples/tutorial/buildings-100.geojson in the globi folder. Click Upload. The page shows 100 rows.
  2. Under 2. Match columns, look at the suggested columns for building ID, number of floors and height. For this file, sbem-ui suggests building_id, num_storeys and height.
  3. Optionally, select id for the building ID. GloBI uses the id column, because semantic-fields.yml names it. Both columns have a unique value for each building.
  4. Under 4. Validate, click Validate. The page shows no issues.

In this tutorial, you use the GIS page only to check the data. GloBI continues to read examples/tutorial/buildings-100.geojson, as set in inputs/my-model/artifacts.yml.

docs.title: Step 5: Semantic Fields
docs.text:
Click Semantic Fields. The page shows the five fields of the tutorial model: Region, Typology, Age_bracket, Income and Scenario. Select a field to see its options. For example, Typology has Office, School, Residential, Hospital and Hotel.

Each option must be in three places:

  1. As a value in the GIS file column with the same name.
  2. In semantic-fields.yml (this page).
  3. In the names of the components that the option selects (step 6).

Thus, a new option (for example Warehouse) also needs warehouse buildings in the GIS file and warehouse components in the component library. For this tutorial, do not change the fields. If you change a field, click Save. To go back to the last saved version, click Revert.

docs.title: Step 6: Component Map
docs.text:
Click Component Map. The component map selects four top-level components for each building. It joins the semantic field values of the building with _ to make each component name:

Component Name built from Example (residential, post-2000, low income, Baseline) Envelope Region, Typology, Scenario, Age_bracket TestRegion_Residential_Baseline_Post_2000 SpaceUse Region, Typology, Income, Scenario TestRegion_Residential_Low_Baseline HVAC Region, Typology, Scenario, Age_bracket TestRegion_Residential_Baseline_Post_2000 DHW Region, Typology TestRegion_Residential

To see the names that a selector builds, click Preview names.

Make a change that GloBI cannot build, and see how the check finds the error:

  1. Under Operations → SpaceUse, remove Income from the fields of the selector.
  2. Click Save & check library. The check reports that all sampled combinations have no record (Library check: ... sampled combinations have no record). It also shows an error like TestRegion_Hotel_Retrofit not found.
  3. Add Income again in its initial position (after Typology).
  4. Click Save & check library again. The check reports Library check passed.

The check fails in step 2 because the map now builds SpaceUse names without Income, such as TestRegion_Hotel_Retrofit. The component library has only TestRegion_Hotel_Low_Retrofit and TestRegion_Hotel_High_Retrofit.

Change the component map when you add components. For example, to give each age bracket its own lighting, create the matching records in the component library. Then add Age_bracket to the selector.

docs.title: Step 7: Component Library
docs.text:
Each top-level component refers to smaller components. For example, a SpaceUse record names its Lighting, Equipment, Occupancy, Thermostat and WaterUse components.

Records can share a smaller component. In the sample component library, all four residential SpaceUse records (low and high income, Baseline and Retrofit) use the same Lighting record, TestRegion_Residential. A change to this record changes all residential buildings in the two scenarios.

Each scenario has its own Thermostat record (TestRegion_Residential_Baseline, TestRegion_Residential_Retrofit). A change to one of these records changes only that scenario. To see the components that a record uses, open the record with Edit. The form shows the linked components by name.

For example, to double the lighting power in residential buildings:

  1. In the sidebar, click Component Library.
  2. Under component types, click Lighting.
  3. Find TestRegion_Residential and click Edit.
  4. Change PowerDensity from 6.5 to 13 (W/m²).
  5. Click Save.

sbem-ui writes the change to inputs/my-model/components-lib.db immediately.

docs.title: One building
docs.text:
make cli-native simulate -- --config examples/tutorial/building.yml --output-dir outputs/model-original
make cli-native simulate -- --config inputs/my-model/building.yml --output-dir outputs/my-model-building

If you run EnergyPlus in Docker, use make cli instead of make cli-native.

Compare the End Uses that the two runs print. Lighting doubles, from approximately 18.7 to 37.4 kWh/m². The total energy increases less, from approximately 176 to 185 kWh/m². The cause is the heat from the lights, which decreases the heating energy.

docs.title: 100 buildings
docs.text:
Start the local stack from section B. Then run:

make cli submit manifest -- --path inputs/my-model/manifest.yml
make cli-native get experiment -- --run-name GloBI_Tutorial_MyModel/Baseline

Before the batch run starts, submit manifest checks that GloBI can build each building from your edited model.

To compare the results with the original run, use the viewer (section E). Open Use Cases → Scenario Comparison and select GloBI_Tutorial/Baseline/... and GloBI_Tutorial_MyModel/Baseline/.... Only the residential buildings change.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Change other components in the same way: window U-values (GlazingConstructionSimple), constructions (ConstructionAssembly), heating and cooling setpoints (Thermostat), schedules (Day, Week, Year).
  • Add a component with + Add .... Then connect a parent record to it. For example, set the Lighting of a SpaceUse record to your new record.
  • Be careful when you rename or delete records. GloBI finds top-level components by name, and parent records refer to child records by name. Save & check library on the Component Map page and submit manifest both find missing components before the simulation starts.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Click a problem to see the cause and the fix.

make setup fails with npm: command not found or node: command not found

Cause: Node.js is not installed, or it is not on the PATH of your terminal.

Fix:

  1. Install Node.js 18 or newer from https://nodejs.org/.
  2. Open a new terminal. On Windows, open a new Git Bash window. In VS Code, restart VS Code.
  3. Run node --version, then run make setup again.
make setup fails at prisma generate

Cause: this step downloads a database engine from the Prisma servers, so it needs internet access. Some university or company networks block the download.

Fix:

  1. Connect to a different network, or turn off the VPN.
  2. Run make prisma-generate again.
  3. If the step fails again, send the full error to the GloBI team.
make setup fails with an error about ../globi

Cause: sbem-ui installs GloBI from a folder with the name globi next to the sbem-ui folder. That folder is missing or has a different name.

Fix:

  1. Put sbem-ui and globi in the same parent folder.
  2. Check that the GloBI folder has the name globi.
  3. Run make setup again.
is not a project workspace (missing project.json) when opening

Cause: the folder path is wrong, or step 2 did not run. If inputs/my-model existed before step 2, cp -r copied the template into inputs/my-model/sbem-project/.

Fix:

  1. Run ls inputs/my-model. The output must show project.json and the files from step 2.
  2. If the files are not there, run rm -rf inputs/my-model. Then do step 2 again (the two cp commands).
  3. Use the absolute path: the output of pwd (or pwd -W on Windows), plus /inputs/my-model.
The Semantic Fields or Component Map page is empty or shows a template picker

Cause: sbem-ui opened a different folder, or the files from step 2 are missing.

Fix:

  1. Check that inputs/my-model/semantic-fields.yml and inputs/my-model/component-map.yml exist.
  2. Open the project again with Open existing.
The page at localhost:5173 does not load, or shows errors when loading

Cause: make dev is not running or stopped with an error, or a different program uses port 5173 or 8000.

Fix:

  1. Look for errors in the make dev terminal.
  2. Check the ports: run lsof -i :8000 on macOS/Linux, or netstat -ano | grep 8000 in Git Bash. Close the other program.
  3. Run make dev again.
Save & check library reports combinations with no record

Cause: the component map builds a name that is not in the component library. For example, you removed a field from a selector, or renamed or deleted a record.

Fix: read the missing name in the error. Then do one of these steps:

  • Change the selector back. Revert goes back to the last saved map.
  • In Component Library, create a record with exactly that name.
Results did not change after editing

Cause: GloBI reads the original files, or the buildings that you ran do not use the record that you edited.

Fix:

  1. Run the configs in inputs/my-model/ (building.yml or manifest.yml), not the configs in examples/tutorial/.
  2. Check that you clicked Save in sbem-ui. Open the record again with Edit to see the saved value.
  3. Use step 6 and step 7 to find the records that the buildings use.
No such file or directory for the model files when using make cli

Cause: Docker can only see inputs/, outputs/, examples/ and tests/data/e2e/. A model in a different folder (for example, your Documents folder) is not available in the container.

Fix: keep the model in inputs/. In the configs, use relative paths like inputs/my-model/components-lib.db.

docs.title: Simulation inputs and outputs
docs.text: This page is the reference for the input files that GloBI reads and the output files that it writes. For a guided run with working example files, see the sample-buildings tutorial.

docs.title: Input files overview
docs.text:
The files that you need depend on the type of run. The tutorial versions of all files are in examples/tutorial/ and tests/data/e2e/.

File Single building Batch run Contents building.yml required -- One building and its semantic field values manifest.yml -- required The experiment and its configs artifacts.yml -- required Paths to the GIS file, model files and weather file semantic-fields.yml required required Semantic fields and the names of GIS columns component-map.yml required required Rules that select components from semantic fields components-lib.db required required The component library (SQLite) GIS file -- required Building footprints and their attributes gis-preprocessor.yml -- optional Geometry checks and default values hourly-data-config.yml -- optional Hourly output variables overheating-config.yml -- optional Overheating thresholds Weather file required required A .zip with the .epw and .ddy files

docs.title: building.yml -- single building specification
docs.text: globi simulate reads this file. For all fields, defaults and an example, see Simulate a single building.

docs.title: manifest.yml -- experiment specification
docs.text:
globi submit manifest reads this file. For the keys, see Batch runs: prepare your inputs.

Each config key (file_config, gis_preprocessor_config, hourly_data_config, overheating_config) accepts a file path or inline YAML. To turn off an optional config, set it to null or leave it out.

Example (examples/tutorial/manifest-overheating.yml):

name: GloBI_Tutorial_Overheating
scenario: Baseline
hourly_data_config: tests/data/e2e/hourly-data-config.yml
file_config: examples/tutorial/artifacts.yml
gis_preprocessor_config: tests/data/e2e/gis-preprocessor.yml
overheating_config: tests/data/e2e/overheating-config.yml

docs.title: artifacts.yml -- file references
docs.text:
The file_config key of the manifest points to this file. For the keys, see Batch runs: prepare your inputs.

If epwzip_file is null and the GIS file has no weather column, GloBI uses the closest TMYx weather file to each building.

Example (examples/tutorial/artifacts.yml):

gis_file: examples/tutorial/buildings-100.geojson
db_file: tests/data/e2e/components-lib.db
semantic_fields_file: tests/data/e2e/semantic-fields.yml
epwzip_file: examples/tutorial/USA_MA_Boston-Logan.Intl.AP.725090_TMYx.2009-2023.zip
component_map_file: tests/data/e2e/component-map.yml

docs.title: semantic-fields.yml -- semantic field definitions
docs.text:
This file defines the semantic fields and names the GIS columns that hold building attributes.

Key Type Required Contents Name str yes Model name Fields list yes The semantic fields Fields[].Name str yes Field name. It must match the GIS column and semantic_field_context keys Fields[].Options list yes Allowed values of a categorical field Fields[].Min, Fields[].Max number yes Allowed range of a numeric field (instead of Options) Building_ID_col str yes GIS column with the building ID Height_col str one of GIS column with the building height [m] Num_Floors_col str these two GIS column with the number of floors WWR_col str no GIS column with the window-to-wall ratio Basement_col, Attic_col str no GIS columns with the basement and attic types Exposed_Basement_Frac_col str no GIS column with the exposed basement fraction Weather_File_col str no GIS column with a weather file for each building GFA_col str no Accepted, but GloBI does not use it

Example (tests/data/e2e/semantic-fields.yml):

Name: Test Region Model
Fields:
  - Name: Region
    Options:
      - TestRegion
  - Name: Typology
    Options:
      - Office
      - School
      - Residential
      - Hospital
      - Hotel
  - Name: Age_bracket
    Options:
      - Pre_1980
      - 1980_to_2000
      - Post_2000
  - Name: Income
    Options:
      - Low
      - High
  - Name: Scenario
    Options:
      - Baseline
      - Retrofit

Height_col: height
Num_Floors_col: num_storeys
Building_ID_col: id

Each building gets one value for each field: from the GIS file in a batch run, or from semantic_field_context in a single-building run. The component map uses these values to select components.

docs.title: component-map.yml -- component selection rules
docs.text:
The component map assigns a selector to each component. The source_fields of a selector list the semantic fields that build the component name.

The file has two top-level sections:

  • Envelope: constructions, windows and infiltration.
  • Operations: space use, HVAC and domestic hot water (DHW).

Example (tests/data/e2e/component-map.yml):

Envelope:
  selector:
    source_fields:
      - Region
      - Typology
      - Scenario
      - Age_bracket

Operations:
  SpaceUse:
    selector:
      source_fields:
        - Region
        - Typology
        - Income
        - Scenario
  HVAC:
    selector:
      source_fields:
        - Region
        - Typology
        - Scenario
        - Age_bracket
  DHW:
    selector:
      source_fields:
        - Region
        - Typology

GloBI joins the field values with _ to make the component name. For example, a residential, post-2000 building in the Baseline scenario gets the Envelope record TestRegion_Residential_Baseline_Post_2000. The record must exist in the component library.

For a more detailed model, give each sub-component its own selector. In the example below, Envelope has separate selectors for Infiltration, Window and Assemblies. The suffix key adds _<suffix> to the end of the name, for example ..._Main.

Envelope:
  Infiltration:
    selector:
      source_fields:
        - Region
        - TypologySpaceUse
        - Weatherization
      suffix: Main
  Window:
    selector:
      source_fields:
        - Region
  Assemblies:
    selector:
      source_fields:
        - Region
        - TypologySpaceUse
        - Age_bracket

Operations:
  SpaceUse:
    Occupancy:
      selector:
        source_fields:
          - Region
          - TypologySpaceUse
    Lighting:
      selector:
        source_fields:
          - Region
          - TypologySpaceUse
          - Lighting
    Equipment:
      selector:
        source_fields:
          - Region
          - TypologySpaceUse
    Thermostat:
      selector:
        source_fields:
          - Region
          - TypologySpaceUse
          - Thermostat
    WaterUse:
      selector:
        source_fields:
          - Region
          - TypologySpaceUse
  HVAC:
    ConditioningSystems:
      Heating:
        selector:
          source_fields:
            - Region
            - Heating
      Cooling:
        selector:
          source_fields:
            - Region
            - Cooling
    Ventilation:
      selector:
        source_fields:
          - Region
          - TypologyVentilation
          - Weatherization
  DHW:
    selector:
      source_fields:
        - Region
        - DHW

To edit the component map in a browser, see Tutorial: edit the model in sbem-ui.

docs.title: components-lib.db -- component library
docs.text:
The component library is a SQLite database with the component records: materials, constructions, windows, HVAC systems, schedules and more. Single-building runs and batch runs use the same file.

The database has one table for each component type:

  • Envelope: ConstructionMaterial, ConstructionAssembly, ConstructionAssemblyLayer, GlazingConstructionSimple, Infiltration, Envelope, EnvelopeAssembly
  • Operations: Occupancy, Lighting, Equipment, Thermostat, WaterUse, SpaceUse, ThermalSystem, ConditioningSystems, HVAC, Ventilation, DHW, Operations
  • Schedules: Day, Week, Year
  • Zone: Zone

The component map selects top-level records by name, for example TestRegion_Office_Baseline_Post_2000. To edit records in a browser, see Tutorial: edit the model in sbem-ui.

docs.title: GIS file -- building footprints
docs.text:
The GIS file holds one row for each building: a footprint polygon and its attributes. GloBI reads any format that GeoPandas reads, for example GeoJSON, GeoParquet or Shapefile. For the required columns, see What a GIS file needs.

Note

tests/data/e2e/buildings.parquet is a GeoJSON file, despite its name.

In a batch run, --scenario sets the Scenario column of all buildings. The value must be one of the options of the Scenario field.

docs.title: gis-preprocessor.yml -- geometry checks and defaults
docs.text:
This file controls how GloBI checks and prepares the GIS file. All keys are optional.

Key Type Default Contents cart_crs str EPSG:3857 Cartesian CRS for geometry operations min_building_area float 10.0 Minimum footprint area [m²] min_edge_length float 3.0 Minimum edge length [m] max_edge_length float 1000.0 Maximum edge length [m] neighbor_threshold float 100.0 Distance to search for neighbor buildings [m] f2f_height float 3.0 Floor-to-floor height [m] min_building_height float 3.0 Minimum building height [m] max_building_height float 300.0 Maximum building height [m] min_num_floors int 1 Minimum number of floors max_num_floors int 125 Maximum number of floors default_wwr float 0.2 Window-to-wall ratio if the GIS file has none default_num_floors int 2 Number of floors if the GIS file has none default_basement str none Basement type if the GIS file has none default_attic str none Attic type if the GIS file has none default_exposed_basement_frac float 0.25 Exposed basement fraction if the GIS file has none epw_query str or null "source in ['tmyx']" Filter for the closest weather file lookup

GloBI ignores other keys. Set the weather file in artifacts.yml, not in this file.

Example (tests/data/e2e/gis-preprocessor.yml, shortened):

cart_crs: EPSG:3857
min_building_area: 10.0
neighbor_threshold: 100.0
f2f_height: 3.0
default_wwr: 0.2
default_num_floors: 2
epw_query: source in ['tmyx']

docs.title: hourly-data-config.yml -- hourly output configuration
docs.text:
This file selects the hourly EnergyPlus variables to report. To turn it on, set hourly_data_config in the manifest. Each variable becomes a separate result table.

Key Type Contents data list[str] Variables to report (see the list below) output_mode str dataframes-and-filerefs, dataframes-only or fileref-only

The available variables are:

  • Zone Mean Air Temperature
  • Zone Air Relative Humidity
  • Zone Mean Radiant Temperature
  • Site Outdoor Air Drybulb Temperature

Example (tests/data/e2e/hourly-data-config.yml):

data:
  - "Zone Mean Air Temperature"
  - "Zone Air Relative Humidity"

output_mode: dataframes-and-filerefs

docs.title: overheating-config.yml -- overheating analysis configuration
docs.text:
This file sets the overheating thresholds. To turn it on, set overheating_config in the manifest. The run then produces the overheating tables. For their contents, see the overheating metrics reference.

Key Type Contents heat_thresholds list Temperatures [°C] for heat exceedance cold_thresholds list Temperatures [°C] for cold exceedance heat_index_criteria dict Hour limits for the heat index categories thermal_comfort dict Thermal comfort assumptions (met, clo, v)

Example (tests/data/e2e/overheating-config.yml):

heat_thresholds:
  - threshold: 26.0
  - threshold: 30.0
  - threshold: 35.0
cold_thresholds:
  - threshold: 10.0
  - threshold: 5.0
heat_index_criteria:
  extreme_danger_hours: null
  danger_or_worse_hours: null
  caution_or_worse_hours: null
thermal_comfort:
  met: 1.1
  clo: 0.5
  v: 0.1

docs.title: How inputs relate to each other
docs.text:
Single building:

building.yml
├── db_file ──────────────► components-lib.db
├── semantic_fields_file ─► semantic-fields.yml
├── component_map_file ───► component-map.yml
└── epwzip_file ──────────► weather file (.zip, local path or URL)

Batch run:

manifest.yml
├── file_config ──────────────────► artifacts.yml
│                                   ├── gis_file ──────────────► GIS file
│                                   ├── db_file ───────────────► components-lib.db
│                                   ├── semantic_fields_file ──► semantic-fields.yml
│                                   ├── component_map_file ────► component-map.yml
│                                   └── epwzip_file ───────────► weather file
├── gis_preprocessor_config ──────► gis-preprocessor.yml
├── hourly_data_config (optional) ► hourly-data-config.yml
└── overheating_config (optional) ► overheating-config.yml

Warning

Write all file paths relative to the repository root, or as absolute paths. For runs with make cli (Docker), keep your files under inputs/: the container only sees inputs/, outputs/, examples/ and tests/data/e2e/.

docs.title: Single building output
docs.text:
globi simulate writes these files to the output folder:

<output-dir>/
├── ep/
│   └── eplus_simulation/
│       ├── Minimal.idf              # generated EnergyPlus model
│       └── {hash}/                  # one EnergyPlus run
│           ├── Minimal.idf
│           ├── *.epw                # weather file used
│           ├── eplusout.sql         # all results (SQLite)
│           ├── eplusout.csv         # output variables
│           ├── eplusmtr.csv         # meter outputs
│           ├── eplustbl.csv         # tabular summary report
│           ├── eplusout.err         # warnings and errors
│           └── ...                  # other EnergyPlus files
└── results/
    ├── EnergyAndPeak.parquet        # main results
    ├── EnergyAndPeak.csv            # one row for each month
    └── EnergyAndPeak.xlsx           # one sheet for each measurement and aggregation

docs.title: Batch run output
docs.text:
globi get experiment downloads one result table for each call:

outputs/
└── {run_name}/
    └── v{version}/
        ├── EnergyAndPeak.pq         # always
        ├── EnergyAndPeak.xlsx       # for EnergyAndPeak only
        └── EnergyAndPeak.csv        # only with --include-csv

To download another table, add --dataframe-key. Other tables are saved as .pq only. For the list of overheating and hourly tables, see section D of the tutorial.

docs.title: EnergyAndPeak table format
docs.text:
EnergyAndPeak is the main output. Its columns have four levels:

Level Name Values 0 Measurement Energy, Peak 1 Aggregation Raw, End Uses, Utilities 2 Meter End uses (Lighting, Equipment, Domestic Hot Water, Heating, Cooling) and fuels (Electricity, NaturalGas, ChilledWater, ...) 3 Month 1 to 12

In a batch run, the row index has building_id and the building features, for example feature.semantic.Typology and feature.geometry.long_edge.

Units: energy in kWh/m², peak in kW/m².

CSV format: the CSV file has one row for each month. The header has four rows, one for each column level:

Measurement  Energy    Energy     Energy              ...
Aggregation  Raw       Raw        Raw                 ...
Meter        Lighting  Equipment  Domestic Hot Water  ...
Month
1            1.588     1.860      1.397               ...
2            1.434     1.680      1.260               ...

Excel format: the workbook has one sheet for each measurement and aggregation:

  • Energy_Raw, Energy_EndUses, Energy_Utilities
  • Peak_Raw, Peak_Utilities
  • Feature Index: building IDs and semantic field values (batch runs only)

docs.title: EnergyPlus raw outputs
docs.text:
The ep/ folder has the EnergyPlus files of a single-building run. The most useful files are:

File Contents Minimal.idf The generated EnergyPlus model *.epw The weather file used eplusout.err Warnings and errors. Read it first if a run fails eplusout.sql All results in one SQLite database eplusout.csv Output variables (temperatures, humidity, energy in joules) eplusmtr.csv Meter outputs (energy by fuel type) eplustbl.csv, eplustbl.htm Tabular summary report (annual totals, end uses) epluszsz.csv Zone sizing data (design loads, mass flows) eplusout.eso EnergyPlus standard output (text) *.eio, *.rdd, *.mdd Variable dictionaries and metadata
